items.title: Lymphatic System Anatomy & Physiology
key_facts: Flow path: initial lymphatics (capillaries) → pre-collectors → collectors (lymphangions) → trunks → thoracic duct → venous angles
Revised Starling Principle: the lymphatic system clears ~100% of interstitial fluid and macromolecules — the venous system does NOT reabsorb fluid at steady state
Resting lymphangion contraction: 6-10 beats/min, can increase ~10x with exercise or MLD
pitfalls: The 'venous reabsorption' trap: assessors ask what % is reabsorbed by veins vs lymphatics. Do NOT say the old 90/10 ratio — correct answer is the glycocalyx layer blocks venous reabsorption, so lymphatics do 100% of the clearance.

flashcards.front: What % of interstitial fluid clearance is done by the lymphatic system under the revised Starling principle?
flashcards.back: 100% — veins do not reabsorb interstitial fluid at steady state

flashcards.front: Resting lymphangion contraction rate?
flashcards.back: 6-10 beats/min, increasing ~10x with exercise/MLD

flashcards.front: Order the lymphatic flow path from capillary to vein.
flashcards.back: Initial lymphatics → pre-collectors → collectors (lymphangions) → trunks → thoracic duct → venous angles

quiz_questions.question: An assessor asks how much fluid venous capillaries reabsorb compared to lymphatics. What's the correct answer?
options: The glycocalyx blocks venous reabsorption — lymphatics do ~100%
It depends on hydrostatic pressure only

items.title: Lymphedema vs. Lipedema — Staging
key_facts: Lymphedema ISL staging: Stage 0 (subclinical, no visible swelling) → I (pits, subsides with elevation) → II (non-pitting, fibrosis) → III (elephantiasis, trophic skin changes)
Lipedema: Types 1-5 (anatomical distribution: I=pelvis/hips, IV=arms, V=lower legs only) and Stages 1-3 (smooth skin → nodular/lobular)
'Stage 4 Lipedema' is outdated — current term is lipo-lymphedema (lymphatic microcirculation is compromised across all lipedema stages, not just end-stage)
pitfalls: Saying 'Stage 4 Lipedema' instead of lipo-lymphedema is an immediate red flag for outdated terminology

flashcards.front: Lymphedema ISL Stage II features?
flashcards.back: Non-pitting, permanent swelling with progressive fibrosis

flashcards.front: What replaced the outdated term 'Stage 4 Lipedema'?
flashcards.back: Lipo-lymphedema

flashcards.front: Lipedema Type I distribution?
flashcards.back: Pelvis/hips

quiz_questions.question: Which lymphedema stage denotes subclinical impaired transport with no visible swelling?

items.title: Classification, Signs & Symptoms
key_facts: Lymphedema: asymmetric, distal-heavy, heaviness not sharp pain, eventual skin thickening, 'peau d'orange' skin
Lipedema: symmetric, halts sharply at ankles/wrists (feet/hands spared), exquisitely tender, bruises easily, palpable nodules
Venous edema: varicosities, hemosiderin staining, medial malleolar ulceration risk, reduces rapidly with elevation
Lipo-lymphedema: adipose lobules mechanically obstruct lymphatics, adding asymmetric fluid/fibrosis onto lipedema
pitfalls: Confusing early venous insufficiency (bilateral, dependency-related, hyperpigmented) with lymphedema
Confusing venous stasis rubor with cellulitis erythema

flashcards.front: Key distinguishing feature: does lipedema involve the feet?
flashcards.back: No — feet/hands are spared, creating a distinct 'cuff' at ankle/wrist

flashcards.front: What does elevation do to venous edema vs. advanced lymphedema/lipedema?
flashcards.back: Venous edema reduces rapidly with elevation; advanced lymphedema/lipedema does not

quiz_questions.question: A patient has symmetric swelling that stops abruptly at the ankles, sparing the feet, with tenderness on palpation. Most likely diagnosis?

items.title: Indications & Contraindications for CDT
key_facts: Absolute contraindications: uncompensated CHF, acute DVT, untreated cellulitis/erysipelas
Neck MLD contraindicated: carotid sinus hypersensitivity, hyperthyroidism, cardiac arrhythmia history
Abdominal MLD contraindicated: pregnancy, aortic aneurysm, recent pelvic surgery, unexplained abdominal pain
ABI < 0.5 = absolute contraindication for compression. ABI 0.5-0.8 = modified short-stretch compression (max 30-40 mmHg working pressure) with close monitoring
pitfalls: The 'treated cellulitis' trap: a patient with cellulitis 3 days ago, on IV antibiotics 48hrs, now afebrile — CDT can carefully resume since it's the UNTREATED acute phase that's contraindicated, not treated/resolving infection

flashcards.front: ABI value that is an absolute contraindication for compression?
ABI range allowing modified short-stretch compression, and at what max pressure?
flashcards.back: 0.5-0.8, max 30-40 mmHg working pressure, with monitoring

flashcards.front: Is treated cellulitis (on antibiotics 48hrs, afebrile) still a contraindication?
flashcards.back: No — untreated acute cellulitis is the contraindication; once actively treated and systemic inflammation has passed, therapy can carefully resume

quiz_questions.question: A patient has an ABI of 0.6. What's the correct compression approach?

items.title: Chart & Record Review
key_facts: For secondary lymphedema: verify ALND vs SLNB, number of nodes excised, radiation fields
ALND + regional radiation: ~40% lymphedema risk. SLNB: <10% risk
Taxane chemo agents cause fluid retention AND peripheral neuropathy — alters compression safety
Must confirm current malignancy status (remission vs active/palliative) before starting CDT
pitfalls: Starting CDT without confirming remission status — active malignant lymphedema needs a modified palliative approach

flashcards.front: Lymphedema risk: ALND + radiation vs. SLNB alone?
flashcards.back: ~40% (ALND+radiation) vs. <10% (SLNB)

flashcards.front: Why do taxane chemo agents matter for compression safety?
flashcards.back: They cause peripheral neuropathy, altering the patient's ability to tolerate/sense compression safely

quiz_questions.question: What critical status must be confirmed before initiating CDT in an oncology patient?

items.title: Comprehensive Patient History-Taking
key_facts: Sudden onset swelling = red flag (vascular occlusion/infection); gradual onset = lymphatic failure
Lymphedema pain: heaviness/tightness/dull ache. Lipedema pain: sharp, exquisitely tender to light touch
Lipedema fat is resistant to caloric restriction and bariatric surgery — key differentiator from obesity
Family history matters for primary lymphedema or hereditary lipedema patterns
pitfalls: Dismissing a high-BMI patient as 'just obesity' without probing for diet/exercise-resistant fat distribution (lipedema)

flashcards.front: What onset pattern is a red flag for vascular occlusion or infection?
flashcards.back: Sudden onset swelling

flashcards.front: Key diagnostic clue distinguishing lipedema fat from obesity?
flashcards.back: Lipedema fat resists caloric restriction and bariatric surgery

items.title: Interdisciplinary Collaboration
key_facts: Vascular surgery: suspected arterial insufficiency (ABI<0.8) or acute DVT
Oncology: sudden hard fixed edema, especially supraclavicular — suggests malignant recurrence
Wound care: copious lymphorrhea, suspected malignant wound transformation, complex venous ulcers
MDT mandatory for Stage III lymphedema and complex lipo-lymphedema (may need surgical debulking/liposuction/lymphovenous anastomosis)
pitfalls: Managing profound lymphorrhea with bandages alone instead of escalating — weeping lymph is a major sepsis risk

flashcards.front: Sudden hard, fixed, non-mobile lymph node — escalate to whom?
flashcards.back: Oncology — suggests active malignancy

flashcards.front: Why is profound lymphorrhea dangerous if managed with bandages alone?
flashcards.back: It's a major risk for sepsis; needs advanced absorbent dressings and possibly wound nursing/antibiotics

items.title: Physical Exam Red Flags
key_facts: Sudden unilateral painful swelling + cyanosis = suspect acute DVT (medical emergency)
Sudden erythema + heat + fever/chills = suspect cellulitis/erysipelas (medical emergency)
Hard, fixed, non-mobile lymph nodes = red flag for active malignancy
Performing MLD on acute DVT or cellulitis risks pulmonary embolism or systemic sepsis
pitfalls: Confusing dependent rubor/lipodermatosclerosis (red, warm, painless, blanches on elevation) with acute infection

flashcards.front: Sudden unilateral painful swelling with cyanosis — suspect what?
flashcards.back: Acute DVT — medical emergency, halt MLD/compression

flashcards.front: Red, warm legs that blanch on elevation and are painless — infection or vascular?
flashcards.back: Vascular (dependent rubor/lipodermatosclerosis), not infection

quiz_questions.question: What is the danger of performing MLD on a patient with acute DVT?

items.title: Neurological Exam
key_facts: Test light touch, pinprick, vibration — especially in chemo patients (taxanes/platinums cause neuropathy)
Absence of protective sensation requires heavy foam padding under compression + patient education on visual skin checks
Motor/reflex testing needed to identify nerve entrapment (e.g., brachial plexus compression from massive limb weight)
pitfalls: Applying standard aggressive short-stretch bandaging to a diabetic or chemo-neuropathy patient without a sensory screen first — automatic fail

flashcards.front: Why must sensory screening precede compression bandaging?
flashcards.back: Absence of protective sensation risks silent pressure necrosis under bandages; requires padding + visual skin check education

items.title: Skin & Limb Assessment
key_facts: Look for loss of Achilles sulcus / transverse palmar arch (contour obliteration)
Brown hemosiderin staining = venous. Extreme pallor = arterial insufficiency. Fiery erythema = infection
Circumferential asymmetry >2cm between limbs at multiple landmarks = clinically significant for unilateral lymphedema
Check interdigital spaces for fungal intertrigo (tinea pedis) — must separate toes to inspect
pitfalls: Failing to separate the toes to check for fungal infection — tinea pedis is the primary entry point for recurrent cellulitis

flashcards.front: What circumferential difference between limbs is clinically significant for unilateral lymphedema?
flashcards.back: >2 cm at multiple anatomical landmarks

flashcards.front: Why must you separate the toes during skin inspection?
flashcards.back: To check for tinea pedis — the primary portal of entry for recurrent cellulitis

items.title: Skin Integrity
key_facts: Lymphorrhea: active weeping of protein-rich lymphatic fluid through micro-fissures (clear-to-amber, beads rapidly) — distinct from serous venous ulcer exudate
Papillomatosis: benign warty cobblestone epidermal outgrowths from chronic inflammation/lymphatic hypertension
Hyperkeratosis: pathological thickening of stratum corneum from failed desquamation
Extensive papillomatosis + hyperkeratosis + deep skin folds = ISL Stage III (Lymphostatic Elephantiasis)
pitfalls: Confusing lymphorrhea with standard venous ulcer exudate

flashcards.front: What three skin findings together confirm ISL Stage III?
flashcards.back: Extensive papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and deep cutaneous folds

flashcards.front: How does lymphorrhea differ from venous ulcer exudate?
flashcards.back: Lymphorrhea is highly proteinaceous, clear-to-amber, beads rapidly from intact-appearing skin/tiny vesicles

items.title: Palpation Technique — Stemmer's Sign
key_facts: Stemmer's sign: pinch/lift skin fold at base of 2nd toe/finger. Positive = fold too thick/rigid/tethered to lift
Positive Stemmer's = highly specific, confirms lymphedema. Negative Stemmer's does NOT rule it out (common false negative in Stage 0/early Stage I before fibrotic remodeling)
Correct technique = pinch and pull UP, not press down (pressing down tests pitting, not Stemmer's)
pitfalls: Pressing down into tissue instead of pinching/lifting — yields false negatives
Assuming negative Stemmer's rules out lymphedema

flashcards.front: Where is Stemmer's sign elicited?
flashcards.back: Base of the 2nd toe or finger

flashcards.front: Does a negative Stemmer's sign rule out lymphedema?
flashcards.back: No — common false negative in ISL Stage 0/early Stage I

quiz_questions.question: A patient's Stemmer's sign is negative. Can you confidently rule out lymphedema?
options: No — false negatives are common in early stages

items.title: Edema Grading
key_facts: Pitting scale: 1+ (~2mm, instant rebound), 2+ (~4mm, <15s), 3+ (~6mm, >1min), 4+ (~8mm, 2-5min)
ISL Stage I pits easily; Stage II/III become non-pitting due to collagen/adipose deposition
Lipedema is classically non-pitting from the outset
pitfalls: Assuming absence of pitting means no edema — both advanced lymphedema and lipedema are non-pitting

flashcards.front: Pitting grade 3+: depth and rebound time?
flashcards.back: ~6mm depth, rebound >1 minute

flashcards.front: Is lipedema typically pitting or non-pitting?
flashcards.back: Non-pitting from the outset

items.title: Measurement Methods
key_facts: Circumferential tape: 4cm intervals, truncated cone formula for volume
Water displacement (volumetry): gold standard for absolute volume, but cumbersome, contraindicated with open wounds

Bioimpedance Spectroscopy (BIS/L-Dex): measures extracellular fluid via electrical resistance; L-Dex change of ~6.5+ units from baseline = subclinical Stage 0 lymphedema, triggers prophylactic intervention
BIS loses accuracy in Stage III fibrotic limbs (fluid replaced by solid fibroadipose tissue)
pitfalls: Using BIS/L-Dex on a Stage III elephantiasis patient — it's not useful there since there's no longer free fluid to measure

flashcards.front: L-Dex change from baseline indicating subclinical Stage 0 lymphedema?
flashcards.back: ~+6.5 units

flashcards.front: Why does BIS lose accuracy in Stage III lymphedema?
flashcards.back: Fluid has been replaced by solid fibroadipose tissue, which BIS can't measure as fluid

quiz_questions.question: A breast cancer patient's L-Dex is +7.0 above baseline but arms look identical. What does this mean?
options: Subclinical Stage 0 lymphedema — early intervention warranted

items.title: Range of Motion Assessment
key_facts: Severe lymphedema creates a 'boggy'/'waterbed-like' soft-tissue-stretch end-feel (fluid blocks joint completion), unlike bony/capsular end-feels
Axillary Web Syndrome (AWS/cording): visible tight fibrous cords from axilla down medial arm post breast-cancer surgery, limits shoulder abduction/flexion
pitfalls: Confusing true capsular pattern (frozen shoulder) with edema-induced mechanical block or AWS

flashcards.front: What is Axillary Web Syndrome and its typical cause?
flashcards.back: Visible/palpable tight fibrous cords from axilla to medial arm, common after breast cancer surgery, limits shoulder abduction/flexion

items.title: Functional & Mobility Impact
key_facts: Lower limb elephantiasis alters center of gravity → lumbar lordosis, circumduction gait
Upper limb fluid obliterates transverse palmar arch, tightens extensor tendons → limits grip/pinch/dexterity
Finger function and thumb opposition are the most critical functional decline markers in UE lymphedema
pitfalls: Focusing care plans only on 'shrinking the limb' rather than restoring functional independence (e.g., dressing)

flashcards.front: Most critical functional decline markers in upper extremity lymphedema?
flashcards.back: Impairment of finger function and thumb opposition

items.title: ADL & Self-Care — Outcome Measures
key_facts: DASH: captures upper limb functional deficits (orthopedic-focused)
LYMQOL: disease-specific, captures physical function + symptoms + body image + psychological distress — superior for lymphedema
Lower Limb Lymphedema Functioning Disability and Health Questionnaire: for lower limb mobility morbidity
PROMs are mandatory, not optional, in value-based healthcare frameworks
pitfalls: Choosing a purely orthopedic scale (DASH) over a multidimensional one (LYMQOL) for a patient with significant psychological distress

flashcards.front: Why is LYMQOL preferred over DASH for lymphedema patients with distress?
flashcards.back: LYMQOL also captures body image and psychological distress, not just physical function

items.title: Goal-Setting & Care Planning
key_facts: Phase 1 (Intensive/Decongestive): clinic-driven, daily sessions 2-4 weeks, max volume reduction, heal lymphorrhea/ulcers, soften fibrosis
Phase 2 (Maintenance): patient-driven, lifelong, sustain reduction via self-management/self-MLD/garments
Stage I goal may be total reversal; Stage III goal shifts to preventing cellulitis and restoring function, NOT full symmetry
pitfalls: Setting 'return limb to normal symmetry, completely cure swelling' as a goal for Stage III — unrealistic, assessors penalize this

flashcards.front: Phase 1 CDT duration and driver?
flashcards.back: Clinic-driven, daily sessions, typically 2-4 weeks

flashcards.front: Realistic primary goal for advanced fibrotic Stage III lymphedema?
flashcards.back: Prevent recurrent cellulitis and restore functional mobility — NOT full symmetry/cure

items.title: Manual Lymphatic Drainage (MLD)
key_facts: Proximal-to-distal clearance: empty central regions (neck/trunk) first to create a vacuum effect, then proximal limb, then distal congested segments
Resting pressure: 30-40 mmHg max. Performed on DRY skin, no oil — oil eliminates the friction needed to stretch/open lymphatics

4 schools: Vodder (light circular/pump strokes, 30mmHg), Földi (Vodder strokes + vigorous medicalized CDT), Casley-Smith (slow effleurage + deep breathing), Leduc (sequential 'call'/'reabsorption' maneuvers)
pitfalls: Using massage oil/lotion during MLD — this is the most common and devastating practical exam failure

flashcards.front: Why is MLD never performed with oil?
flashcards.back: Oil eliminates the friction needed to stretch skin and open initial lymphatics, making treatment ineffective

flashcards.front: MLD clearance direction principle?
flashcards.back: Proximal-to-distal: clear central regions first to create a vacuum, then move distally

flashcards.front: Which MLD school uses sequential 'call' and 'reabsorption' maneuvers?
flashcards.back: Leduc

quiz_questions.question: Why is central torso/unaffected quadrants treated before the swollen limb during MLD?
options: It feels better for the patient
To create a negative pressure gradient / suction effect for the congested fluid to move into

items.title: Soft Tissue & Peripheral Joint Mobilization
key_facts: Full-range muscle contraction is the primary extrinsic driver of lymphatic transport — stiff joints impair pumping
Deep soft tissue mobilization (breaking fibrotic cross-links, AWS cording release) must only happen AFTER central pathways are cleared via MLD
pitfalls: Aggressive deep friction massage on fragile lymphedematous skin — high capillary fragility risks hematoma/cellulitis

flashcards.front: Sequencing rule: MLD vs. deep tissue mobilization for fibrotic tissue/AWS release?
flashcards.back: MLD (central clearance) must happen first, before deep soft tissue mobilization

items.title: Compression Garments & Padding
key_facts: Phase 1: short-stretch bandages (Rosidal K, Comprilan) — low extensibility (30-60%), low resting pressure (safe overnight), high working pressure (muscle pump wall)
Long-stretch (e.g. ACE wrap) has dangerously high resting pressure — NOT appropriate for CDT, risks ischemia especially overnight
RAL-GZ 387 classes (ankle pressure): Class I 18-21 mmHg, Class II 23-32 mmHg, Class III 34-46 mmHg, Class IV >49 mmHg
pitfalls: Suggesting an ACE wrap (long-stretch) as a budget substitute for short-stretch bandages — absolute NO, risks ischemia

flashcards.front: RAL Class II ankle pressure range?
flashcards.back: 23-32 mmHg

flashcards.front: Short-stretch bandage: resting pressure vs. working pressure?
flashcards.back: Low resting (safe overnight), high working (muscle pump against rigid wall)

flashcards.front: Is an ACE wrap (long-stretch) acceptable for Phase 1 CDT?
flashcards.back: No — dangerously high resting pressure, risks ischemia

quiz_questions.question: What ankle pressure range defines a RAL Class II compression garment?

items.title: Posture & Body Mechanics Education
key_facts: Tight bra straps, heavy bags, restrictive waistbands occlude superficial lymphatic collectors
Elevate limb above heart level, joints slightly flexed
Elevation is effective in Stage I (free fluid responds to gravity) but ineffective in Stage III (solid fibroadipose tissue doesn't respond to gravity)
pitfalls: Recommending nightly elevation as a 'sufficient care plan' for Stage III elephantiasis — ineffective at that stage

flashcards.front: Why is elevation ineffective for Stage III lymphedema?
flashcards.back: The limb mass is mostly solid fibroadipose tissue, which doesn't respond to gravity

items.title: Therapeutic Exercise
key_facts: Diaphragmatic breathing = 'thoracic duct pump': deep inhale drops diaphragm → negative intra-thoracic + positive intra-abdominal pressure → vacuum draws lymph up through thoracic duct
Decongestive exercises MUST be done wearing compression — forces muscle to expand inward against veins/lymphatics rather than outward
Progressive/monitored weightlifting is SAFE and does not exacerbate lymphedema — this is a modern evidence-based correction of an old myth
pitfalls: Believing heavy resistance training triggers/worsens lymphedema — this is an outdated myth assessors use as a trap

flashcards.front: What mechanism does diaphragmatic breathing use to move lymph?
flashcards.back: The 'thoracic duct pump' — negative intra-thoracic/positive intra-abdominal pressure creates a vacuum drawing lymph up centrally

flashcards.front: Must decongestive exercise be performed with or without compression?
flashcards.back: With compression — forces muscle expansion inward against lymphatics/veins

flashcards.front: Is progressive weightlifting safe for lymphedema patients?
flashcards.back: Yes — current evidence shows it's safe and doesn't exacerbate lymphedema, refuting an old myth

quiz_questions.question: Explain the mechanism of the 'thoracic duct pump' via breathing.
options: Deep inhalation creates a pressure differential that acts as a vacuum, drawing lymph from lower body/mesenteric basins into the thoracic duct
It only works if done for 1 hour

items.title: Patient, Family & Caregiver Education
key_facts: Skin/nail care: low-pH, unscented lotions to preserve the acid mantle and prevent fissures
Untreated tinea pedis (athlete's foot) = leading portal of entry for recurrent cellulitis in LE lymphedema
Teach garment donning/doffing/laundering and modified self-MLD (opening central pathways daily)
pitfalls: Prescribing a rigid Class III circular-knit stocking to a patient with arthritis/low grip strength without considering Velcro-wrap alternatives or donning aids

flashcards.front: Leading portal of entry for recurrent cellulitis in lower limb lymphedema?
flashcards.back: Untreated tinea pedis (athlete's foot)

items.title: Documentation Standards
key_facts: Must capture: circumferential/volume changes, L-Dex trends, skin integrity changes, adverse events, PROM (LYMQOL) trends over time
Benchmark for clinical efficacy: 10% reduction in relative limb volume, or L-Dex regression below the 6.5 threshold
Baseline measurements MUST be documented before starting MLD — without a baseline, efficacy can't be proven (clinical governance violation)
pitfalls: Failing to document baseline measurements prior to starting treatment

flashcards.front: Benchmark limb volume reduction indicating successful decongestion?
flashcards.back: 10% reduction in relative limb volume (or L-Dex back below 6.5)

items.title: Communication Standards
key_facts: Requires empathy, expectation management, shared decision-making — these are chronic, incurable, progressively disfiguring conditions
Lipedema patients often endure years of medical gaslighting ('just eat less, exercise more') — validate that it's a distinct, diet-resistant connective tissue disorder
Avoid paternalistic dictation of care plans; partner with the patient on what's functionally/socially tolerable
pitfalls: Dictating a rigid care plan without considering the patient's real-world tolerance (e.g., garment thickness in Dubai heat)

flashcards.front: What common experience do lipedema patients often report from prior healthcare providers?
flashcards.back: Medical gaslighting — being told to just diet/exercise more, despite it being a distinct diet-resistant disorder

items.title: Scope of Practice (UAE / DHA)
key_facts: Governing document: DHA Scope of Practice for Physiotherapist (Code: DHA/HRS/HPSD/SP-07)
Physiotherapists are autonomous practitioners but must refer out for diagnosing DVT, confirming malignancy, or treating sepsis — outside PT scope
DHA Law No. (14) of 2021 governs health regulation and PQR (Professional Qualification Requirements)
PTs cannot advise on medication changes (e.g., diuretic dosing) — must refer back to the attending physician
pitfalls: Offering any pharmacological advice (e.g., 'should I increase my diuretic') — must always refer to the physician

flashcards.front: Can a UAE physiotherapist diagnose a DVT?
flashcards.back: No — must screen for red flags and refer to vascular/medical evaluation, diagnosis is outside PT scope

flashcards.front: What DHA code governs physiotherapist scope of practice?
flashcards.back: DHA/HRS/HPSD/SP-07

quiz_questions.question: A patient asks if they should increase their diuretic dose. What should the PT do?
options: Refuse to alter medication and refer back to the attending physician

items.title: Professional Accountability
key_facts: Credentials require Primary Source Verification (PSV) via DataFlow Group
DHA mandates 20 accredited CPD points annually for license renewal
Passing the Prometric exam only yields an Eligibility Letter — active license requires linking to a DHA-licensed employing facility via the Sheryan portal
pitfalls: Assuming passing the Prometric exam alone grants authority to practice — it doesn't, until linked via Sheryan

flashcards.front: How many CPD points must DHA-licensed Allied Health Professionals log annually?
flashcards.back: 20 accredited CPD points

flashcards.front: What does passing the Prometric exam alone grant?
flashcards.back: Only an Eligibility Letter — not an active license (requires facility linkage via Sheryan)

rapid_recall.fact: Revised Starling Principle: 100% of tissue fluid is reabsorbed by the lymphatic system; veins do not reabsorb.
Lymphedema = ISL Stages 0-III. Lipedema = Types 1-5, Stages 1-3. 'Stage 4' is now termed Lipo-lymphedema.
Stemmer's Sign: Negative in Lipedema, Positive in Lymphedema. Lipedema spares hands/feet.
ABI < 0.5 is an absolute contraindication for compression bandaging.
Axillary node clearance + regional radiation = high risk of secondary lymphedema (~40%).
Sudden unilateral swelling+pain = suspect Acute DVT; localized heat/fever = suspect Cellulitis.
Papillomatosis & Hyperkeratosis indicate Stage III fibrotic skin breakdown (Elephantiasis).
Elicited at base of 2nd toe/finger. False negative common in early clinical stages.
L-Dex change of +6.5 units from baseline = subclinical lymphedema requiring immediate intervention.
Vodder: 30mmHg circular. Casley-Smith: effleurage over lymphotomes. Foldi: medical CDT focus.
Short-stretch bandage: high working pressure, low resting pressure — safe for overnight wear.
Diaphragmatic breathing creates negative intra-thoracic pressure, pumping the central thoracic duct.
Autonomous practice within scope; 20 CPD points/year required for license renewal.

reference_tables.title: Lymphedema vs. Lipedema vs. Venous Edema

assessor_probe_questions.question: Patient has ABI of 0.6 — compression approach?
assessor_probe_questions.model_answer: ABI 0.6 = moderate PAD. ABI<0.5 is absolute contraindication; 0.5-0.8 allows modified short-stretch compression, max 30-40mmHg, with heavy padding and monitoring for ischemia.

assessor_probe_questions.question: Stemmer's sign negative — can you rule out lymphedema?
assessor_probe_questions.model_answer: No. High specificity, low sensitivity early on. Common false negative in ISL Stage 0/early I before fibrotic remodeling.

assessor_probe_questions.question: Short-stretch vs long-stretch — why use one over the other in CDT?
assessor_probe_questions.model_answer: Short-stretch: low resting pressure, high working pressure — muscle pump wall. Long-stretch: high resting pressure (arterial risk), low working pressure — not appropriate for CDT.

assessor_probe_questions.question: Why treat central torso/unaffected quadrants before the swollen limb in MLD?
assessor_probe_questions.model_answer: Proximal-to-distal clearance principle — empties central reservoirs first to create a negative pressure/suction gradient for congested fluid to move into.

assessor_probe_questions.question: Bilateral symmetric leg swelling, tender, easy bruising, ankle cuff, normal feet — diagnosis?
assessor_probe_questions.model_answer: Classic lipedema presentation — foot sparing, tenderness, symmetry, bruising distinguish it from lymphedema.

assessor_probe_questions.question: Sudden unilateral warmth, erythema, fever — immediate action?
assessor_probe_questions.model_answer: Suspect acute cellulitis/erysipelas — medical emergency, absolute contraindication for MLD/compression. Halt treatment, escalate immediately.

assessor_probe_questions.question: Explain the Thoracic Duct Pump mechanism.
assessor_probe_questions.model_answer: Diaphragmatic breathing generates negative intra-thoracic + positive intra-abdominal pressure, creating a vacuum drawing lymph from lower body/mesentery up through the thoracic duct into the venous angles.

assessor_probe_questions.question: Can you diagnose a DVT under DHA scope?
assessor_probe_questions.model_answer: No — diagnosing acute pathology exceeds PT competency. Screen for red flags and refer for vascular medical evaluation.

assessor_probe_questions.question: L-Dex +7.0 above baseline, arms look identical — what does it indicate?
assessor_probe_questions.model_answer: Subclinical (ISL Stage 0) lymphedema — extracellular fluid accumulation not yet visible/measurable by tape. Warrants early intervention (mild compression sleeve).

assessor_probe_questions.question: RAL Class II garment — ankle pressure range?
